title: Say little, do much (Avot 1:15)
hookLine: Shammai: make study regular, say little and do much, greet everyone cheerfully
last: CARE FOR YOURSELF, CARE BEYOND YOURSELF.

lines: A LITTLE SOMETHING, A WHOLE TRAY.
A SAYING THAT ENDS WITH A SMILE.
cards: Two guests, one party. The first says, I'll bring a little something, and walks in with a tray of food that feeds the whole room. The second promises the moon in the group chat, and shows up with a bag of ice.
Today's sage is Shammai, Hillel's partner in the chain. Later stories give him a reputation as the strict one, the one with the short temper, and you'll meet one of those stories in a few weeks.
So his saying is a surprise. It ends with a smile.

teach.b: Shammai's saying has three parts. First: make your Torah fixed. Set a regular time for study and keep it, instead of learning only when you happen to feel like it.
Second: say little and do much. The Talmud finds the model in Abraham.

teach.h: A MORSEL OF BREAD, THEN A FEAST.
teach.b: Three strangers come to his tent in the heat of the day, and he offers them, in his words, just a morsel of bread. Then he runs to the herd for a tender calf, has cakes baked from fine flour, and brings curd and milk.
He promised a snack and served a feast. The rabbis say that's how the righteous behave: they promise a little and do a lot.
Third, the surprise from the strict one: receive every person with a cheerful face.
The Hebrew is be'sever panim yafot, literally with a pleasant, beautiful face. Every person, not only your friends or the important ones.

An early rabbinic collection goes further: give someone the best gifts in the world with a sour face, and it's as if you gave nothing; greet them warmly with empty hands, and it's as if you gave them everything.
A steady habit, quiet follow-through, and a warm face at the door.

And that closes a week of sages: judge people favorably, kindness isn't the same as closeness, a question can teach a lie, half a wage, just to listen, pursue peace, care for yourself, care beyond yourself, and today, say little, do much.

how: A fixed daily or weekly time for Torah study, often with a study partner, is a long-standing Jewish practice, and 'receive everyone with a cheerful face' is taught as basic Jewish courtesy.

o: only help people who have helped you first
promise a little, then do far more than you said
promise big, so people know how much you care

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: then a calf, cakes, curd and milk

s: the strict Shammai said to greet every person cheerfully
receive every person with a cheerful face is the end of his saying.
Abraham promised the strangers a feast
he offered just a morsel of bread, then served a calf, cakes, curd and milk.
a gift given with a sour face counts the same
an early rabbinic teaching says it's as if you gave nothing at all.

games.q: you're Abraham. three strangers arrive at your tent in the heat of the day. what do you say?
o: come in, I'll make you a great feast.
let me bring you a morsel of bread.
there's a well down the road.
games.why: he offered a morsel of bread, then ran for a calf and fine flour. the rabbis learn from him: say little, do much.

practice: Notice what your face is doing right now, maybe a little tight around the eyes, and let your jaw loosen and your forehead go soft.
Then think of the next person you'll see, and picture greeting them the way you'd greet someone you've missed. Hold that picture, and let the warmth reach your face.

wordCard.voice: Say little. Shammai's rule, learned from Abraham: promise a little, do a lot, and greet every person with a cheerful face.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: say little and do much.

carryVoice: Your line: just a morsel of bread. Then came the whole feast. Two hundred forty-five days now.
